logline: Nate blows his mom's money on AirPods to resell, gets three days to sell them and is thrown out when he can't; a friend in a supercar runs over his stock, takes his laptop and 'scales it', and when his mom pulls up beside their supercar at a red light he tells her 'We scaled it.'

hook.mechanic: Title caption 'Mom said we'd fail' + a mom-vs-son shouting match already in progress: she screams about her money, dumps a whole bin of AirPods on his bed, rapid-fire insults and a 'Three days... or you're out' ultimatum. One locked-off set-up for 10.6 s, stitched from three clips with a duvet wipe and a smear cut; pace comes from dialogue (about 4.8 words per wall-clock second) and big physical comedy, not cutting.
hook.first_line: Nate! Where did all my money go? You spent it on these?

montage.description: Grind/waiting montage (9.25 s, 14 shots, median 0.54 s) with one-word VO beats: cleaning AirPods at a desk as the window light jumps from morning to golden hour, phone 'POST' UI insert, deadpan 'Nothing', whip into a mini softbox photo studio ('Better pictures'), then a locked-off wide time-lapse in a storage room - the same chair and pose cut or dissolved through day / sunset / night / white-flash day / night / sunset / night - while he counts 'Soon. Zero. Come on. No. One. Just one.' and the AirPod piles grow into mountains around him. The light change IS the edit device.

stats.dead_air: None in the audio sense: a music/SFX bed runs the full 56 s (silencedetect -35 dB/0.4 s found no silence). Gaps with no dialogue (>=1.5 s): 10.31-12.89 (2.6 s), 13.69-16.03 (2.3 s), 38.71-42.10 (3.4 s), 45.96-48.44 (2.5 s), 49.88-51.40 (1.5 s).

beats.summary: HOOK: Mom finds where her money went - AirPods everywhere; she dumps a bin of them on his bed and gives him three days to sell them.
Grind/waiting montage: cleaning, posting, better photos, time-lapse of waiting through days and nights; 'Zero... One... Just one.'
'Yes!' - one sale; mom bursts in: 'Out! Pack!' - he's on the doorstep with a suitcase: 'Bro, these things ruined my life.'
Inciting accident: a red supercar runs over one of his AirPods; 'Ah! Bro!' - the friend steps out.
Banter two-shot: 'It's not funny.' 'It's a little funny.' - friend roasts his method, takes his laptop: 'Watch.'
Scaling: time-lapse at the laptop, dashboards climb; 'I scale brands.' 'Scale it.' 'Say less.' - crash zoom into Nate's screaming mouth.
Success: supercar flames out down a city street, pedestrians stare, Nate riding shotgun: 'Bro, this thing is insane.'
Reversal: at a red light Mom pulls up in a beaten beige sedan - 'Nate? Is that you? How did you even make it?' - 'We scaled it.'
Real-me tag: 5 handheld live-action flex clips (boat with both creators, supercar exhaust, warehouse, balcony, garage).

transcription: faster-whisper small (CPU, int8), word timestamps; cross-checked against burned-in captions in 0.1-0.15 s strips. 'Nate!', 'Ah!', 'Bro, what do you do?', 'Nate?' (at the light) and 'Say less' corrected/added from captions.
why_it_works: Title caption 'Mom said we'd fail' promises the payoff and, with 'we', sets up the collab before the friend appears.
Hook is pure performance in one held set-up: a dumped bin of AirPods is a big, readable visual gag, and the dialogue is fast and quotable, with a clear deadline ('Three days... or you're out').
The waiting montage uses a locked-off frame and time-of-day lighting jumps (day / sunset / night) plus growing piles of stock, so time passing and failure read with no explanation.
Comedy carries the low point: 'Bro, these things ruined my life', then the supercar literally runs over his stock - the meet-cute with the mentor is an accident.
The collab partner is introduced as aspiration (scissor-door supercar, iced chain) and given the cool lines ('It's a little funny', 'Say less'), so the guest creator looks good.
Long 6 s banter two-shot lets the jokes breathe, then the edit speeds up for the scaling payoff (dissolve time-lapse at the laptop -> crash zoom into the mouth -> black -> exhaust flames).
The 'into the mouth/black/new scene' transition is a strong reusable device for a jump in status.
The reversal mirrors the opening: the same mom now in a dented beige sedan beside the red supercar - a status flip told in one wide frame at a red light.
Three-word payoff 'We scaled it' echoes the post caption and the friend's 'Scale it', tying story, collab and CTA together.
1.45 s real-life tag (opening on both creators on a boat) grounds the CG fable in their real lifestyle and loops quickly.
undetermined: Music not identified; a music/SFX bed runs under the whole reel (silencedetect -35 dB / 0.4 s found no silence).

Second creator: the post caption tags @brezscales and the CG friend is the mentor who scales the business; that the CG friend and the curly-haired man in the boat tag clip are @brezscales is inferred, not confirmed.

Whisper's 5.88 words/s draft rate: the captions confirm almost every word was really spoken, so the word count holds; the rate is high because whisper's line spans are tight around fast, overlapping dialogue. Our corrected figure uses the same method (words / summed line spans) for consistency with the fomo example. As a wall-clock check, the 0.05-10.31 s argument has 49 words in 10.26 s = about 4.8 words/s.

Caption-only additions: 'Nate!' (0.05 s, whisper heard 'Wait'), 'Ah!' (~28.3 s), 'Bro, what do you do?' (42.1-43.2 s, missed by whisper), 'Nate?' before 'Is that you?' (~51.4 s). 'Say less' corrected from whisper's 'Stay left'. Timings estimated from caption changes.
'Better pictures' (13.35 s) and 'Dude!' (38.41 s) have no caption; kept from audio, speaker uncertain for 'Dude!'.
'Exactly, bad example.' (6.79 s) speaker split unclear; probably Nate 'Exactly', then mom 'Bad example'.

Shot 1-3 (0-10.57 s, auto-detected as one 10.6 s shot): checked by eye - same locked camera, but joined by a duvet-swipe wipe at 2.0 s and a smear/ghost cut with a time jump (bin teleports to the floor) at 7.25 s; counted as 3 shots. If those are read as in-shot moves, the shot count drops by 2.
Character drift: in the time-lapse (shots 14-19) Nate's cap disappears and his hair reads curlier - an AI-generation consistency slip, not a story choice.
Montage boundaries are a judgement call (the time-lapse dissolves are counted as shots).
